squat.label: Squat (bilateral knee-dominant)
squat.doThisNotThat: Sit down between your feet with the torso staying stacked over mid-foot, not a hip-back good-morning that dumps the load into your lower back.
squat.priorityNote: Athleticism wins: crisp reps that stop at ~20% speed loss beat grinding to failure, even though grinding adds a little volume for size.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop the set when rep speed visibly slows (~20% velocity loss)
prescription.slot: Main lift, right after the CNS prime
prescription.warmup: 1 set × 6-8 at ~50% of working load, same tempo

defaultSteps: Feet shoulder-width, toes out 10-20°, weight on the tripod.
Brace: big breath into belt line, ribs down, then do the Screw.
Descend 2-3 s, knees forward over toes as far as heels stay down; hips drop between heels.
At the bottom (thighs at or below parallel), drive up as fast as possible, keeping chest and hips rising together.
defaultCues: Spread the floor apart with your feet
Push the floor away as fast as you can
Keep the bar over the middle of your foot

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical load through the spine; ground reaction force must stay over mid-foot or the moment arm on the hip or knee explodes.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Knees ~110-130° flexion at depth, hips ~100-120°, ankle dorsiflexion ~30-35° (your stiffness limits this).
biomechanics.momentArm: Horizontal distance from load to knee (quads) and to hip (glutes/spine). More forward knee travel = more quad moment arm; more hip-back = more hip moment arm.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot → ankle → knee → hip → trunk. Arch collapse makes the knee cave (valgus) and the hip rotate in, wasting force sideways.
biomechanics.grf: Newton's 3rd law: push the floor straight down and it pushes the load straight up. If force drifts to the toes, the bar drifts forward and the back takes over.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Just above parallel (~90° knee) — the "sticking region" where quad and glute moment arms are both near their maximum.

neural.intent: Lower under control, then try to throw the floor down. Max intent on every rep even if the bar moves slowly — intent drives fast-twitch recruitment.
neural.rfd: Rate of force development is what transfers to jumping and first-step speed; it improves when you lift with max intent and stop before reps slow down a lot.

powerPair.rest: ~4-8 min after the heavy set (PAPE); 20-30 s would be contrast

squat.mobility: Full-depth loaded squats build ankle dorsiflexion and hip flexion range about as well as stretching (Afonso 2021). Pause 2 s at the bottom on warm-up sets to let your stiff ankles and hips release.
squat.footBase: Tripod foot (big-toe ball, pinky-toe ball, heel) + the Screw: rotate both feet outward into the floor without letting them move. The arch lifts, the shin stops rolling in, the knee tracks over the 2nd-3rd toe and the glutes switch on. Your flat feet are where force leaks first — set this before every rep, not just the first.

looks.effect: Quads (especially vastus lateralis/medialis for the "teardrop") and glutes. Builds the lower half so legs match the upper body.
looks.lengthened: Deep squats load the quads at long muscle length; heels-elevated or front squats bias the deep-knee position that grows the distal quad.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Vertical force production for jumps, first steps and level changes; heavy leg strength improves running economy for XC.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Squat strength under a brace = stable stance and powerful level changes for shots and sprawls.

intensityTechnique.technique: None on heavy free-weight squats unless you have safeties; on machine/hack squat: one rest-pause (10-15 breaths) on the last set

tips.tip: Stop the set when a rep visibly slows. 20% velocity loss gave a bigger jump gain (+9.5% vs +3.5%) than grinding to 40%, with 40% fewer reps.
Rest 2.5-3 min. Longer rest between sets gave more strength and thigh muscle in trained lifters than 1 min.
If your heels lift or your knees cave, put 1-2 cm plates under your heels. That compensates for stiff ankles instead of letting the arch collapse.
Heavy squats + plyos make running cheaper for XC — your leg day is running training.

squat.teachMe: Your nervous system only releases deep range when it trusts the base. Flat feet send a "danger" signal — the arch collapses, the knee caves and the brain cuts force to protect the joint. The Screw rebuilds the base so the brain lets the quads and glutes fire fully. Physics does the rest: push straight down through mid-foot and the ground pushes back straight up the chain.

swaps.home: Goblet squat or DB front squat with heels elevated, 3 s down + 1 s pause, or 1.5-rep squats to make light dumbbells hard.
swaps.bodyweight: Heels-elevated tempo squat (4 s down, 2 s pause) or jump squat for power.

hinge.label: Hinge (deadlift / RDL family)
hinge.doThisNotThat: Push your hips back to a wall behind you with soft knees and a long spine, not a squat-down with the bar drifting away from your legs.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop the set when rep speed visibly slows (~20% velocity loss)
prescription.slot: Main lift, right after the CNS prime
prescription.warmup: 1 set × 6-8 at ~50% of working load, same tempo

defaultSteps: Bar or dumbbells over mid-foot, feet hip-width, tripod set.
Soft knees (~15-20°), brace, lats pulled down ("bend the bar").
Push hips back, weight drifting toward heels, bar sliding down the thighs until you feel a strong hamstring stretch (usually mid-shin).
Drive hips forward to stand tall; squeeze glutes, ribs stay down — don't lean back.
defaultCues: Push your hips back to the wall behind you
Keep the bar dragging up your legs
Push the floor away and snap the hips through

biomechanics.forceVector: Load hangs vertically; the hip is the hinge point, so torque on the hip = load × horizontal distance from bar to hip.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hips flex to ~70-90°, knees only ~15-30°, spine neutral (not flexed).
biomechanics.momentArm: Every cm the bar drifts forward adds hip and low-back moment. Keeping it touching your legs is free strength.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet → hamstrings/glutes → spinal erectors (isometric) → lats (keep bar close) → grip.
biomechanics.grf: Push down and slightly back through mid-foot/heel; that ground force becomes horizontal hip drive — the same vector as sprint acceleration.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Bottom stretch (hamstrings longest, hip moment arm largest) — for RDLs; floor break for deadlifts.

neural.intent: Slow, controlled eccentric to the stretch, then an aggressive hip snap. On deadlifts, pull the slack out before the floor break.
neural.rfd: Fast hip extension is the motor behind sprinting, jumping and punching from the ground up.

powerPair.exercise: Kettlebell or DB swing, or Broad Jump

hinge.mobility: RDLs to a deep hamstring stretch build hamstring length under load — strength through range improves ROM about as much as stretching (Afonso 2021). For your stiffness, add a 2 s pause at the bottom of warm-up reps.
hinge.footBase: Tripod foot (big-toe ball, pinky-toe ball, heel) + the Screw: rotate both feet outward into the floor without letting them move. The arch lifts, the shin stops rolling in, the knee tracks over the 2nd-3rd toe and the glutes switch on. Your flat feet are where force leaks first — set this before every rep, not just the first.
hinge.sequencing: Hips lead, bar follows: hips and shoulders rise together off the floor; the lockout is a hip snap, not a lean-back.

looks.effect: Hamstrings, glutes and erectors — the side view of the legs and a thick lower back for posture.
looks.lengthened: RDLs load the hamstrings at long length, which is where growth stimulus is strongest.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Hip extension power for acceleration, jumps, throwing and swinging; hamstring strength protects against strains.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Hinge strength = lifting and finishing takedowns, posture in the clinch, and resisting being bent over.

intensityTechnique.technique: None on heavy deadlifts. On RDLs: last set add 3-5 lengthened partials in the bottom half

tips.tip: Stop at 1-2 reps in reserve; failure on heavy hinges costs power and technique for almost no extra growth.
For RDLs, depth is set by your hamstrings, not the floor. When your pelvis starts tucking under, that's the bottom.
Trap bar deadlift is the best default for an athlete: more upright torso, less back stress, fastest bar speeds.
Rest 2.5-3 min between heavy sets.

hinge.teachMe: The hinge is your engine's on-switch: hip extension produces the horizontal force that drives sprinting and the rotation that starts a punch. Physics: the bar's distance from your hip is a lever arm — keep it short and the same muscles move more weight. Neurologically, a stiff, protective body hates the stretched position; slow, controlled exposure teaches it that range is safe.

swaps.home: Single-leg DB RDL (3 s down, 1 s pause) — halves the load you need. Or B-stance RDL.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg RDL reach with a 3 s lowering, or hip hinge with a broomstick on your back.

single-leg.label: Single-leg (lunge / split squat / step-up)
single-leg.doThisNotThat: Drop the back knee straight down with the front foot screwed in, not a lunge forward where the front knee caves in and the heel lifts.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop the set when rep speed visibly slows (~20% velocity loss)
prescription.slot: Main lift, right after the CNS prime
prescription.warmup: 1 set × 6-8 at ~50% of working load, same tempo

defaultSteps: Stance long enough that the front shin can travel forward with heel down.
Front foot: tripod + Screw; hold weights at your sides or goblet.
Lower 2-3 s until the back knee is 2-5 cm off the floor.
Drive through the whole front foot to stand; finish tall with ribs down.
defaultCues: Drop the back knee straight down toward the floor
Push the floor away through your front heel and big toe
Keep the front knee over your middle toes

biomechanics.forceVector: Mostly vertical through the front leg; torso lean shifts load from quad (upright) to glute (leaning ~30°).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Front knee ~90-110° at bottom, front hip ~80-100°, back hip in extension (hip-flexor stretch).
biomechanics.momentArm: Short stance = more forward knee = quad moment; long stance + lean = hip moment.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Single foot → ankle → knee → hip → trunk. Every link must stabilize sideways too (frontal plane), which is exactly where flat feet fail.
biomechanics.grf: One foot handles ~85-90% of the load, so ground force must be centered on the tripod or the knee wobbles in.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The bottom 1/3 when the front knee is most bent and the glute is longest.

neural.intent: Controlled down, explode up; own the bottom without wobbling.
neural.rfd: Single-leg force production is how every sport actually happens — cutting, jumping off one leg, pushing off in boxing.

powerPair.rest: ~4-8 min (PAPE) or right after the set (contrast)

single-leg.mobility: The back leg gets a loaded hip-flexor stretch every rep — directly attacks the anterior hip tightness that comes with all-over stiffness. Front leg builds ankle dorsiflexion.
single-leg.footBase: Tripod foot (big-toe ball, pinky-toe ball, heel) + the Screw: rotate both feet outward into the floor without letting them move. The arch lifts, the shin stops rolling in, the knee tracks over the 2nd-3rd toe and the glutes switch on. Your flat feet are where force leaks first — set this before every rep, not just the first. Single-leg work exposes it most: if the arch drops, the knee follows within milliseconds.

looks.effect: Quads and glutes, with balanced left/right development.
looks.lengthened: Deep BSS loads the front glute and quad long; Pedrosa 2022 found lengthened-range training favorable for distal quads.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Every stride, cut, layup and lunge for a ball is single-leg. Fixes left/right asymmetries and frontal-plane knee control.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Stance strength and the penetration step for shots; one-leg stability when defending a single leg.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials in the bottom half (3-5) or 1.5-rep style

tips.tip: Light dumbbells? Use a 3 s lowering, 1.5 reps or a deficit — single-leg work doubles the effective load on each leg.
Lean the torso ~30° forward for glutes; stay upright for quads.
Training at long muscle lengths gave favorable quad adaptations vs short ranges.
Do your weaker leg first and match reps on the stronger side.

single-leg.teachMe: Single-leg work trains the balance system and the strength system at the same time. The brain has to solve stability in three planes, so it fires the hip abductors and foot muscles that flat feet leave sleeping. Once the base is stable, the brain stops braking and lets the big muscles produce force — that's why single-leg strength shows up fast on the court.

swaps.home: Bulgarian split squat with DBs (3 s down) or deficit reverse lunge.
swaps.bodyweight: Bulgarian split squat with 4 s lowering, or skater squat to a pillow.

knee-flexion.label: Knee flexion (leg curls / Nordics)
knee-flexion.doThisNotThat: Curl with your hips pinned down and toes pulled up, lowering for 3 s — not hips lifting off the pad and the weight dropping.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR on early sets; last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lowering, 1 s pause in the stretch, controlled-fast up
prescription.slot: Accessory block, after main lifts and power work

defaultSteps: Set the pad just above the heels/Achilles, knee joint lined up with the machine axis.
Grip the handles and pin hips to the pad (seated: lap pad tight on thighs).
Pull toes up toward the shins, curl fast to full flexion, 1 s squeeze.
Lower 3 s to a full stretch without letting the stack touch.
defaultCues: Pull the pad to your butt
Keep your hips glued to the pad
Lower like the weight is twice as heavy

biomechanics.forceVector: Resistance acts at the ankle, perpendicular to the shin; the hamstrings pull the tibia back via a short lever behind the knee.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Knee from ~0-10° to ~120-130° flexion. Hip angle changes the length: seated (hip flexed ~90°) keeps hamstrings longer than lying.
biomechanics.momentArm: The machine cam or your body angle sets it; Nordics have the longest lever (your whole body) near full extension.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Knee-flexor isolation; gastrocnemius helps unless you keep the ankle dorsiflexed hard.
biomechanics.grf: No ground force on machines; Nordics/slider curls use your bodyweight against gravity anchored at the ankles.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Machines: near full extension (stretched). Nordics: the last 30° before your chest hits the floor.

neural.intent: Explode into flexion, resist the lowering. Eccentric hamstring strength is what protects sprinting.
neural.rfd: Fast knee-flexion torque decelerates the shin at the end of every sprint stride — the moment most hamstring strains happen.

knee-flexion.mobility: Seated curls and Nordics take the hamstrings to long length under load, which builds usable range in your stiff hamstrings.
knee-flexion.footBase: Standing curls: tripod + Screw on the standing foot, glute squeezed so the pelvis doesn't tilt.
knee-flexion.footBaseSeated: Pull toes up hard (dorsiflex) to reduce calf help and put the work on the hamstrings. Feet stay neutral, not turned out.

looks.effect: Hamstring thickness for the side view of your thighs; balances quad-heavy legs.
looks.lengthened: Seated leg curls (hips flexed = hamstrings stretched) grew hamstrings more than lying curls (Maeo et al. 2021).

sportTransfer.mechanism: Eccentric hamstring strength brakes the swing leg at top speed; Nordics cut hamstring injury risk.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Strong hamstrings help pull the hips through on takedowns and protect knees in scrambles.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials (3-5 half reps in the stretched half) after the last full rep; or one drop set of ~25-30% load

tips.tip: Pick seated over lying when you can — seated leg curls grew the hamstrings more because the hip position keeps them stretched.
Programs with Nordic hamstring curls reduced hamstring injuries by up to ~51% (≈45% in the low-bias studies). 2 × 4-6, 1-2x/week is enough.
Pull the toes up. A pointed foot lets the calves steal the curl.
Near-failure works as well as failure for growth; save true failure for the last set.

knee-flexion.teachMe: Your hamstrings cross two joints, so their length depends on the hip AND the knee. Flexing the hip (seated curl) pre-stretches them, and muscles grow more when loaded long. Neurologically, eccentric strength is a braking skill — the nervous system only lets you sprint at speeds it knows it can stop.

swaps.home: Single-leg slider or towel curl on a smooth floor, or a DB held between the feet lying face-down.
swaps.bodyweight: Nordic curl with feet anchored under a couch (band-free), or slider/towel hamstring curls.

knee-extension.label: Knee extension (leg extensions / sissy squats)
knee-extension.doThisNotThat: Kick up fast and lower 3 s into the deep-bent position with hips pinned back — not short, bouncy reps that skip the bottom half.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR on early sets; last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lowering, 1 s pause in the stretch, controlled-fast up
prescription.slot: Accessory block, after main lifts and power work

defaultSteps: Set the seat so your knee joint lines up with the machine pivot; back rest so your hips are fully back.
Pad on the lower shin just above the ankle; grip the handles to stay pinned.
Extend to full lockout fast, 1 s squeeze at the top.
Lower 3 s to a deep bend (~90° or more) without the stack touching.
defaultCues: Kick the pad to the ceiling
Keep your hips glued to the seat
Let the pad sink all the way back

biomechanics.forceVector: Resistance acts at the shin perpendicular to the tibia; the quads pull through the patellar tendon.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Knee from ~90-100° flexion to 0°. Rectus femoris is lengthened more if you lean back (hip extended).
biomechanics.momentArm: Lever from knee axis to the pad; the machine cam usually keeps tension through the range.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Pure quadriceps isolation — no foot, hip or trunk demands, which makes it a clean way to add quad volume.
biomechanics.grf: None on the machine; sissy squats and reverse Nordics use bodyweight with knees as the pivot.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Varies with the cam; often near lockout. Sissy squats and reverse Nordics are hardest deep (stretched).

neural.intent: Explode into the extension, control the return. Fast knee extension is the final link of a jump or sprint push.
neural.rfd: Knee extension torque contributes to jumping and decelerating; useful but secondary to multi-joint work.

knee-extension.mobility: Deep-flexion reps and reverse Nordics load the quads and rectus femoris long, easing the front-of-thigh and hip-flexor stiffness that limits your stride.
knee-extension.footBase: Standing variants (sissy squat, Spanish squat, TKE): tripod foot and a Screw before every rep — the knee travels far forward, so the arch has to hold.
knee-extension.footBaseSeated: Toes pulled slightly up and pointing straight ahead; feet don't flare out.

looks.effect: Quad sweep and the teardrop (vastus medialis) above the knee.
looks.lengthened: Leaning back during leg extensions puts rectus femoris at longer length; prioritize the deep half of the range.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Quad and patellar-tendon strength for landing, deceleration and kicking.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Knee robustness for stance work and level changes.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials (3-5 half reps in the stretched half) after the last full rep; or one drop set of ~25-30% load

tips.tip: Spend your effort in the deep half: lengthened-range training gave favorable quad growth.
Lean the torso back 10-20° (or recline the seat) to stretch rectus femoris, the only quad muscle squats barely grow.
Knee pain? Use a slower 3 s lowering and a range that's pain-free, then build it out. Sharp or joint-line pain = stop and swap.

knee-extension.teachMe: Squats grow the vasti but under-train rectus femoris, because it shortens at the hip as it lengthens at the knee. Leg extensions isolate the quads so the nervous system can send all its drive to one muscle group without the balance and foot demands that limit you elsewhere.

swaps.home: Sissy squat holding a doorframe, or DB-between-feet seated extensions.
swaps.bodyweight: Reverse Nordic (kneeling lean-back) or sissy squat.

calf.label: Calf raise (plantarflexion)
calf.doThisNotThat: Pause 2 s at the very bottom stretch and rise through the big toe, not fast bouncy reps in the top half.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR on early sets; last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2 s up, 2 s pause at the bottom stretch, 2 s down
prescription.slot: Accessory block, after main lifts and power work

defaultSteps: Balls of the feet on a step edge, heels hanging.
Lower to the deepest stretch you can and pause 2 s.
Rise straight up through the big-toe side as high as possible, 1 s squeeze.
Lower 2 s back to the stretch.
defaultCues: Drive the big toe through the floor
Reach the top of your head to the ceiling
Sink the heel to the floor and wait

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical; the foot is a lever with the ball of the foot as the fulcrum and the Achilles pulling the heel up.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Ankle from ~20-30° dorsiflexion (stretch) to ~40° plantarflexion. Straight knee = gastrocnemius; bent knee (seated) = soleus.
biomechanics.momentArm: Achilles moment arm ~4-5 cm; the load sits over the ball of the foot, so the muscle force is ~2-3× bodyweight per rep.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot arch → ankle → Achilles → calf. A rolled-in ankle (flat foot) shifts load to the outer calf and weakens the push.
biomechanics.grf: Force through the forefoot; centering it on the big-toe side keeps the ankle from rolling out.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The bottom stretch (most load on the Achilles); the top for the squeeze.

neural.intent: Rise with intent, but the gains are in the controlled stretch.
neural.rfd: Stiff, strong calves store and return energy on every stride and jump.

calf.elastic: Heavy calf work stiffens the Achilles tendon, making it a better spring. Pair with pogos so the stiffness becomes fast elastic return, not just strength.
calf.mobility: The 2 s bottom pause is loaded ankle dorsiflexion — the exact range your stiff ankles lack for deep squats and low athletic stances.
calf.footBase: Short-foot: before each rep, gently pull the ball of the foot toward the heel to lift the arch, then rise through the big toe. Flat feet roll out at the top; the big-toe cue fixes that.
calf.footBaseSeated: Balls of the feet on the plate, arch lifted (short-foot), push through the big toe.

looks.effect: Calf size and shape, which balances the lower leg for shorts.
looks.lengthened: Lengthened partials (bottom half only) grew the medial gastrocnemius more than full ROM (Kassiano 2023).

sportTransfer.mechanism: Ankle stiffness and push-off force for sprinting, jumping and staying on the balls of your feet.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Bouncy footwork and pivoting on the ball of the foot for hooks all run on calf endurance.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials in the bottom half after failure (5-10)

tips.tip: Bottom-half partials grew the medial gastrocnemius more than full range.
Do both: straight-knee (gastrocs) and bent-knee (soleus). Soleus takes the most load when running.
Add tibialis raises (toes up against a wall) for shin health on XC mileage.

calf.teachMe: The Achilles is a spring: the stiffer and stronger it gets, the more energy it gives back each ground contact, which lowers the oxygen cost of running. The long bottom pause also calms the protective reflex that keeps your ankles stiff, so the brain learns that deep dorsiflexion is safe.

swaps.home: Single-leg calf raise on a stair holding one dumbbell.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg calf raise on a stair with a 2 s bottom pause.

glute-bridge.label: Hip thrust / glute bridge
glute-bridge.doThisNotThat: Finish with ribs down and chin tucked, shins vertical, squeezing glutes — not arching your lower back to get the hips higher.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop the set when rep speed visibly slows (~20% velocity loss)
prescription.slot: After main lifts, before isolations
prescription.warmup: 1 set × 6-8 at ~50% of working load, same tempo

defaultSteps: Upper back on a bench at the bottom of the shoulder blades, feet flat ~hip-width.
Load across the hip crease (pad it).
Ribs down, chin tucked, push through heels until hips are level with knees and shins are vertical.
Hold 1 s squeezing glutes, lower 2 s.
defaultCues: Push the floor away through your heels
Keep your eyes on the wall in front, not the ceiling
Drive your hips up to the ceiling

biomechanics.forceVector: Horizontal relative to your body (anteroposterior) — the same direction as sprint acceleration force.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hips from ~90-100° flexion to 0-10° extension; knees ~90° at the top.
biomechanics.momentArm: Load sits right on the hip, so glute torque is highest at full extension.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet → hamstrings/glutes → pelvis; trunk braces so the lower back stays neutral.
biomechanics.grf: Pushing through heels directs ground force into hip extension rather than knee extension.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Lockout (full hip extension), where the glutes are shortest.

neural.intent: Drive the hips up hard, pause, control down.
neural.rfd: Hip extension speed shows up in acceleration and in the rear-hip drive of a cross.

glute-bridge.mobility: Full hip extension at the top stretches the hip flexors — useful for the anterior hip tightness that comes with your stiffness.
glute-bridge.footBase: Standing variants (cable pull-through, kickback): tripod + Screw on the standing foot. On bridges/thrusts, push through the heels and the big toe, arches lifted.
glute-bridge.footBaseSeated: Feet flat, ~hip-width, tripod pressure through heel and big toe; knees track over the 2nd-3rd toe, don't let them cave in.
glute-bridge.sequencing: Hips lead: posterior pelvic tilt and glute squeeze first, then the trunk follows. Same hip-snap that powers punches and throws.

looks.effect: Glute size and shape, posture.
looks.lengthened: Bridges load the glutes short; pair with deep single-leg work or RDLs for the stretched position.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Horizontal hip extension power for acceleration; glute strength stabilizes the knee against valgus.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Bridging power for escapes (upa) and hip drive when finishing a double leg.

intensityTechnique.technique: Rest-pause (10-15 breaths) or 10 s isometric hold at lockout

tips.tip: Tuck the chin and look forward; it locks the ribcage down so the glutes do the work instead of the lower back.
Strong glutes help hold the knee out on landings — a fix for flat-foot knee cave.
Glute bridges load the glutes short; combine with RDLs or split squats for full-range development.

glute-bridge.teachMe: Your glutes are the biggest force producers you have, and in a protective, stiff body they often fire late. The thrust trains them to fire hard at full hip extension, where sprinting and punching need them. Physics: the force direction is horizontal, which squats don't train.

swaps.home: Single-leg hip thrust off the couch with a DB on the hip, 2 s pause at the top.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg glute bridge with a 3 s top hold.

hip-abduction.label: Hip abduction
hip-abduction.doThisNotThat: Lean slightly forward and push the knees out against the pad with a 2 s hold — not a fast flapping motion with the lower back arched.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR on early sets; last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lowering, 1 s pause in the stretch, controlled-fast up
prescription.slot: Accessory block, after main lifts and power work

defaultSteps: Machine: sit tall or lean ~20° forward, pads outside the knees.
Push the knees out as wide as possible, 1-2 s hold.
Return slowly, 2-3 s, without the stack touching.
defaultCues: Push the pads apart
Knees out toward the walls
Hold the squeeze for a full second

biomechanics.forceVector: Lateral (frontal plane).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hip abduction ~0-45°. Flexing the hip (leaning forward) biases glute max upper fibers; neutral biases glute medius.
biomechanics.momentArm: Load acts at the knee (machine) or ankle (band/side-lying) — ankle = longer lever, harder.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Glute medius/minimus stabilize the pelvis on one leg; weak = hip drop and knee cave.
biomechanics.grf: Standing versions: the stance leg must hold the pelvis level against gravity.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Full abduction (shortest position) for most machines; the start for bands.

neural.intent: Controlled, full squeeze; feel the side of the hip.
neural.rfd: Not a power movement; builds the stabilizer that lets you cut and land without the knee caving.

hip-abduction.mobility: Full range abduction under control opens the inner hip and teaches the brain to own the frontal plane.
hip-abduction.footBase: Standing (band walks, cable abduction): tripod + Screw on the stance foot; the Screw itself switches on these same muscles.
hip-abduction.footBaseSeated: Feet flat on the rests, toes forward; push through the outer heel.

looks.effect: Upper glute shape and hip width.
